title: Genetic instrumental variable analysis: Time to call Mendelian randomization what it is. The example of alcohol and cardiovascular disease

claims.statement: In adults without heart disease when they joined prospective cohort studies, mostly in high-income countries, drinking a little compared with not drinking is associated with less coronary heart disease, but how much less depends on who is counted as not drinking, and no paper read gives absolute risks, so the ratios cannot be turned into numbers out of 100. Against non-drinkers as each study defined them (in most studies people not drinking at the start, including former drinkers), people who drank had pooled relative risks of 0.71 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.77) for new coronary heart disease (29 studies) and 0.75 (0.68 to 0.81) for coronary death (31 studies); at 2.5 to 14.9 g of ethanol a day (up to about one drink, counted as 12.5 g where a study gave no grams) the figures were 0.75 (0.65 to 0.88) and 0.79 (0.73 to 0.86), below 2.5 g a day 0.96 (0.86 to 1.06) and 0.92 (0.80 to 1.06), and at every higher intake, up to more than 60 g a day, 0.66 to 0.79; 8 of the 84 cohort reports gave only unadjusted estimates (Ronksley et al., 2011). In the 7 to 9 studies that compared with lifetime abstainers the figures were similar (0.73, 0.61 to 0.88; 0.75, 0.66 to 0.85), and former drinkers had more coronary deaths (1.31, 1.02 to 1.68; against non-drinkers in the paper's table, against people who drank in its text). A review that compared only with lifetime abstainers and kept men, women, deaths and new cases apart (Roerecke & Rehm, 2012; 24 studies) found lower point estimates at about one drink of 12 g a day in all four groups, but men's coronary deaths were not clearly lower at about one or two drinks a day (0.89, 0.79 to 1.00; 0.86, 0.73 to 1.02) and women's were not lower at about two drinks (1.03, 0.84 to 1.27); with all 44 studies, including those that combined men and women or deaths and new cases, every estimate at about one to three drinks a day was lower (0.62 to 0.81), and occasional drinking (less than weekly, or under 2.5 g a day) was not associated with coronary risk in any group. Of 23 conditions in the GBD 2016 curves fitted to 592 studies, only ischaemic heart disease showed a significant dip, lowest at 0.83 drinks of 10 g a day in men (relative risk 0.86, 95% uncertainty interval 0.80 to 0.96) and 0.92 in women (0.82, 0.72 to 0.95). Self-reported drinking showed the same dip in Chinese men (Millwood et al., 2019) and in UK Biobank, where allowing for smoking, body mass index, physical activity, cooked vegetable and red meat intake and self-rated health removed the statistically clear difference at moderate intake (more than 8.4 to 15.4 US drinks of 14 g a week) and, read approximately from the paper's figure, reduced but did not remove it at light intake (Biddinger et al., 2022). Whether alcohol causes the lower risk is disputed: in the same team's earlier review, cited second-hand, former drinkers had more coronary deaths than lifetime abstainers (men 1.25, women 1.54), and in men drinking 60 g a day or more the lower risk seen against current non-drinkers (0.75, 0.63 to 0.89) was not seen against lifetime abstainers (1.00, 0.74 to 1.36; Roerecke & Rehm, 2014); genetic studies do not find the lower risk (see the answer on gene studies). Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Ronksley et al. 2011 (prospective cohorts to September 2009; against non-drinkers as each study defined them, mostly current non-drinkers including former drinkers; each study's most-adjusted estimate, unadjusted for 8 of 84): any drinking, incident CHD RR 0.71 (0.66–0.77; 29 studies), CHD mortality 0.75 (0.68–0.81; 31), CVD mortality 0.75 (0.70–0.80; 21); I² 72.2%. By intake (under 2.5, 2.5–14.9, 15–29.9, 30–60, over 60 g/day): incident CHD 0.96 (0.86–1.06), 0.75 (0.65–0.88), 0.66 (0.59–0.75), 0.67 (0.56–0.79), 0.76 (0.52–1.09); CHD mortality 0.92 (0.80–1.06), 0.79 (0.73–0.86), 0.79 (0.71–0.88), 0.77 (0.72–0.83), 0.75 (0.63–0.89). Against lifetime abstainers: incident CHD 0.73 (0.61–0.88; 9 studies), CHD mortality 0.75 (0.66–0.85; 7), CVD mortality 0.82 (0.78–0.86; 9). Former drinkers (against non-drinkers by the table, against drinkers by the text): CHD mortality 1.31 (1.02–1.68), CVD mortality 1.48 (1.23–1.79), incident CHD 1.10 (0.91–1.33). Roerecke & Rehm 2012 (44 studies to April 2010; against lifetime abstainers; former drinkers excluded and mortality corrected for them): fully stratified studies at 2.5–11.99, 12–23.99, 24–35.99 g/day, men's IHD mortality 0.89 (0.79–1.00), 0.86 (0.73–1.02), 0.78 (0.63–0.97); men's morbidity 0.77 (0.65–0.92), 0.75 (0.64–0.88), 0.74 (0.53–1.02); women's mortality 0.84 (0.74–0.96), 1.03 (0.84–1.27), 0.89 (0.57–1.40); women's morbidity 0.54 (0.45–0.65), 0.61 (0.38–0.99), 0.40 (0.14–1.13); occasional drinking 0.82 to 0.98, none significant; all 44 studies 0.62 to 0.81, every interval excluding 1 (occasional 0.87 to 0.97, none significant); I² up to 84%. GBD 2016 (592 studies; against each study's non-drinking category, adjusted for former drinkers in it): IHD minimum RR 0.86 (95% UI 0.80–0.96) in men at 0.83 and 0.82 (0.72–0.95) in women at 0.92 standard drinks (10 g) a day; no significant dip for any other of 23 outcomes. UK Biobank (Biddinger et al. 2022): J- or U-shaped conventional associations; the moderate-intake difference for coronary artery disease not significant after six lifestyle factors (no values printed). China Kadoorie Biobank men (Millwood et al. 2019): conventional U shape for heart attack and CHD (no values printed for non-drinkers). Second-hand (Roerecke & Rehm 2014): former drinkers against lifetime abstainers, IHD mortality men 1.25 (1.15–1.36), women 1.54 (1.17–2.03); men drinking 60 g/day or more, IHD mortality 1.00 (0.74–1.36) against lifetime abstainers, against Ronksley et al.'s 0.75 (0.63–0.89) against current non-drinkers above 60 g/day. No absolute risks in any paper read.

claims.statement: In people of European descent and in Chinese men, genetic variants that predict more drinking, compared with variants that predict less, are associated with more coronary heart disease in the European studies but not with heart attacks in the Chinese study; in its main analysis none of the four genetic studies read found lower coronary risk with genetically higher intake, none can show the shape of the curve at low intake with confidence, and a published critique argues that such studies remain observational and have biases of their own. No study gives absolute risks. In 56 European-descent studies (261,991 people), carriers of a variant of the alcohol-metabolising gene ADH1B reported 17.2% less drinking (95% CI 15.6% to 18.9%) and had lower odds of coronary heart disease (odds ratio 0.90, 0.84 to 0.96; 20,259 events); the authors had predicted that a protective effect of light to moderate drinking would show as higher odds in carriers who drank lightly to moderately, but the odds were similar at every level of drinking and each of those estimates was compatible with no difference (more than 0 to under 7 UK units of 7.9 g a week, 0.90, 0.79 to 1.02), and the variant went with lower blood pressure even in people who said they did not drink (Holmes et al., 2014). In UK Biobank (371,463 people), a genetic score built from variants for alcohol use disorder was associated with coronary artery disease, odds ratio 1.38 (1.10 to 1.74) per standard deviation of genetically predicted intake (a unit the paper does not define), and curves fitted with a method whose key assumption was not tested rose from the first drink, though a second score suggested no rise below roughly 7 to 14 drinks of 14 g a week, with slight decreases at modest intake for hypertension and in some analyses in women (Biddinger et al., 2022). In European summary data with up to 94 variants, the odds ratio was 1.16 (1.00 to 1.36) per standard deviation of log drinks a week and 1.08 (0.91 to 1.27) after allowing for genetic liability to smoking, which the variants also predicted; the ADH1B variant alone was associated with coronary artery disease (Larsson et al., 2020). In 161,498 genotyped Chinese adults, men's genotype-predicted mean intakes (4 to 256 g a week by group) were not associated with heart attack (relative risk 0.96, 0.78 to 1.18, per 280 g a week, which is 40 g a day; 1,696 cases) or with coronary heart disease (1.05, 0.94 to 1.17), although self-reported drinking in the same men showed lower heart-attack rates at moderate intake than in non-drinkers (Millwood et al., 2019). Three epidemiologists (Mukamal, Stampfer & Rimm, 2020; no funding or interests statement printed) argue that such analyses can be biased by ancestry, by parents' genes and drinking, by weak links between genes and reported intake, by genes that act through acetaldehyde rather than amount, by lowering heavy drinking days together with average intake, and by testing lifelong rather than adult drinking; they quantify none of these and report no figures from the studies they criticize, and Roerecke and Rehm (2014) likewise set the ADH1B result aside because the variant also lowers binge drinking. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Holmes et al. 2014 (56 studies, 261,991 European-descent people; ADH1B rs1229984 A-allele carriers against non-carriers): weekly intake 17.2% lower (15.6% to 18.9%), binge drinking OR 0.78 (0.73–0.84), abstention 1.27 (1.21–1.34); coronary heart disease OR 0.90 (0.84–0.96; 20,259 events; I² 17%), 0.81 (0.72–0.91) in four studies with at least 1,000 events; self-reported non-drinkers 0.98 (0.88–1.10), drinkers 0.86 (0.78–0.94), difference P = 0.095; light (more than 0 to under 7 UK units/week of 7.9 g) 0.90 (0.79–1.02), moderate (7 to under 21) 0.89 (0.75–1.06), heavy (21 or more) 0.97 (0.76–1.24), trend P = 0.83; systolic blood pressure in self-reported non-drinkers −0.80 mm Hg (−1.41 to −0.19); no instrumental-variable estimate. Biddinger et al. 2022 (UK Biobank, 371,463; 5-variant score for alcohol use disorder, F 780; OR per SD of genetically predicted intake): coronary artery disease 1.38 (1.10–1.74; P = .006), myocardial infarction 1.37 (1.05–1.78; P = .02, above the paper's threshold of P < .008); nonlinear: quadratic fit best (P < .001), risk rising from zero intake with the primary score; secondary score: no rise until roughly 7 to 14 drinks (14 g) a week. Larsson et al. 2020 (up to 94 variants; per SD of log drinks/week): coronary artery disease 1.16 (1.00–1.36; P = 0.052), 1.08 (0.91–1.27) adjusted for genetic liability to smoking initiation; never-smokers 1.39 (0.98–1.96); instrument and smoking initiation OR 1.24 (1.15–1.33); ADH1B variant alone, positive (P < 0.05). Millwood et al. 2019 (China Kadoorie Biobank men; six genotype–area groups, mean intake 4 to 256 g/week; per 280 g/week, which is 40 g/day): myocardial infarction RR 0.96 (0.78–1.18; 1,696 cases), coronary heart disease 1.05 (0.94–1.17; 6,145 cases); single variants (GG against AG) myocardial infarction rs671 1.02 (0.92–1.13), rs1229984 1.11 (0.95–1.31); women 0.94 (0.74–1.20). Mukamal et al. 2020: no estimates. No absolute risks in any study.

claims.statement: In people averaging less than 30 g of ethanol a day, in seven observational studies pooled by one team, drinking heavily on some occasions compared with drinking the same average amount without such occasions is associated with a higher risk of ischaemic heart disease (deaths and new cases combined); no absolute risks are given. Against lifetime abstainers, people without heavy drinking occasions had a pooled relative risk of 0.64 (95% CI as printed 0.53 to 0.71, an interval that does not fit its point estimate on the log scale, so one figure is probably misprinted; editors' calculation) and people with them 1.12 (0.91 to 1.37), that is, no lower risk than lifetime abstainers; the ratio between the two groups was 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25) (Roerecke & Rehm, 2014). The same team's earlier review, cited second-hand, gave 1.45 (1.24 to 1.70) for people with irregular heavy drinking occasions against people who drank without them. The article does not say what counted as a heavy drinking occasion, which seven studies were pooled or how many people and events they included (all only in a supplement not read); all seven adjusted for age and smoking, one author searched for and extracted the studies, and their risk of bias was not assessed. The review of average intake against lifetime abstainers and the GBD 2016 model did not take drinking pattern into account, and genetic variants that lower average intake also lower heavy drinking (odds of binge drinking 0.78, 0.73 to 0.84, in carriers of the ADH1B variant; Holmes et al., 2014), so two critiques argue that the genetic studies may partly reflect heavy drinking days rather than average amount (Roerecke & Rehm, 2014; Mukamal et al., 2020). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
claims.magnitude: Roerecke & Rehm 2014 (seven studies; against lifetime abstainers; ischaemic heart disease mortality and morbidity combined; most-adjusted estimates, all adjusted for age and smoking): average under 30 g/day without heavy drinking occasions RR 0.64 (0.53–0.71 as printed; geometric midpoint of that interval 0.61, editors' calculation), I² 10%, Egger P = 0.35; with heavy drinking occasions 1.12 (0.91–1.37), I² 0%, Egger P = 0.58; ratio with against without 1.75 (1.36–2.25), equal to 1.12/0.64 (editors' arithmetic), method of its interval not described. Roerecke & Rehm 2010, as cited by Roerecke & Rehm 2012: RR 1.45 (1.24–1.70), drinkers with irregular heavy drinking occasions against drinkers without them. Holmes et al. 2014: ADH1B intake-lowering variant, binge drinking OR 0.78 (0.73–0.84) and 17.2% fewer UK units a week. No absolute risks, numbers of participants or events, or definition of a heavy drinking occasion in the article.
